research_notes: Year 1879 is the premiere year: first performed 1 January 1879 at the Liceo Artístico y Literario de Matanzas; conventionally regarded as the first danzón. Alejo Carpentier (quoted by Radamés Giro via IPS Cuba) dates Faílde's manuscripts of this and three other danzones to June 1877. Named after the Simpson neighbourhood of Matanzas.

Composition year 1910 per English Wikipedia (citing Odilio Urfé 1965). Urfé added a final montuno section borrowed from son, an important step in the danzón's evolution. Urfé played clarinet in Enrique Peña's orchestra (photo caption on Wikipedia); the association of the first performance with Peña's orchestra is inferred from that and is not separately confirmed. Cubadebate feature is titled after the piece.
Composition year 1929 per English Wikipedia (citing Odilio Urfé 1965): Díaz added a sung part to the danzón, creating the danzonete. Only one source consulted.

original_instruments: Flute | Violins | Piano | Double bass | Timbales | Güiro
research_notes: Composition year differs between sources: 1938 (getbailar) and 1937 (Leonardo Padura, IPS Cuba), so year left empty. Cubadebate calls it the most-recorded danzón of all time. Valdés later named his charanga orchestra Almendra after it. Instrumentation listed is the standard charanga line-up described by getbailar, not a documented first-recording personnel.

Granma gives 1938 as the composition year of Orestes López's 'Mambo (danzón with son rhythms)', start of the 'nuevo ritmo'. English Wikipedia confirms Orestes López devised the mambo section and that his danzón 'Mambo' started a trend continued by Arcaño y sus Maravillas. Considered a seed of the later mambo genre.

original_instruments: Violins | Flute | Piano | Double bass | Tumbadora | Timbales | Güiro
research_notes: Composed by Jorrín in Havana in 1951 (first performed that year); year 1953 is the release year of the Panart 78 rpm (Panart 1536, recorded March 1953), widely considered the first cha-cha-chá record. Original label billed it as 'mambo-rumba'. Instrumentation from the session personnel listed on Spanish Wikipedia (Álex Sosa, piano).
B-side of 'La engañadora' (Panart 1536, 1953 release), billed on the label as danzón. Spanish Wikipedia states the name 'cha-cha-chá' came from this song's refrain. English title in original.

secondary_associations: United States (rumba craze) | Don Azpiazú and His Havana Casino Orchestra | Antonio Machín
research_notes: Dates conflict: Library of Congress says Rita Montaner made the first recording in Havana in 1927; Granma says Simons wrote it in 1928; a Library of Congress manuscript on Internet Archive is dated 1928-02-11 and tagged piano/vocal (so a voice-and-piano manuscript may exist, not confirmed). Don Azpiazú's New York recording (May 1930, vocal Antonio Machín) launched the US 'rumba' craze and was added to the National Recording Registry in 2005. The LOC essay notes the lyrics' authorship is debated (Fernando Ortiz claimed a real vendor wrote them). Technically a son-pregón, not a rumba.

title_english: Put a Little Sauce on It
original_format: Septeto (vocals, guitar, tres, trumpet, bass, bongó, maracas, claves)
research_notes: Written 1930 (UCSB DAHR biography: on a train to Chicago) and premiered by the Septeto Nacional around 1931 (Son Soneando blog). Earliest recording found: Cuarteto Machín, 28 Feb 1933 (DAHR matrix BS-75333); La Jiribilla says the Septeto Nacional did not record it until 1958. Its opening motif was used by Gershwin in his Cuban Overture (1932). Inspired by the butifarra sausages of 'El Congo' in Catalina de Güines.
Year 1930 is the recording year: DAHR lists a Cuarteto Machín recording of 14 July 1930 (matrix BVE-62792, Piñeiro as composer) and La Jiribilla lists 'Suavecito. Septeto Nacional, 1930'.

original_format: Vocal trio/quartet with guitars and trumpet
secondary_associations: Son cubano | Dominican Republic (place of composition)
research_notes: Year 1931 is the recording year: Victor matrix XVE-67176, recorded in Havana 24 Feb 1931 by the Cuarteto Matamoros (Matamoros, Rafael Cueto, Siro Rodríguez, trumpeter Pedro Vía) per UCSB DAHR. Composition date varies by source (1928, 1929 or 1930); written in Santo Domingo. Cubarte (citing María Teresa Linares) notes it was not the first bolero-son but the most famous.

original_format: Vocal with guitars and son ensemble
secondary_associations: Buena Vista Social Club (1997 album) | Eliades Ochoa
research_notes: Year 1984 is the composition year (Wikipedia and New York Times; SecondHandSongs gives 1987). First recorded 1985 by Compay Segundo's group; internationally famous through the Buena Vista Social Club recording (recorded March 1996, released 1997).

Year 1946 is the composition year (Wikipedia, El País, The Guardian). El País says RCA Victor first recorded a version in 1947 and the song spread through the Mexican film 'Callejera'. Emblem of the filin movement (jazz-influenced Cuban romantic song).

composer: Vincent Ford (credited); Bob Marley (widely attributed melody/authorship, disputed)
original_instruments: vocals | guitar | bass guitar | drums | Hammond organ
research_notes: Released 25 October 1974 on Natty Dread (Island/Tuff Gong), recorded at Harry J Studio, Kingston. Official writing credit: Vincent 'Tata' Ford. Multiple sources (including a 1975 JBC interview cited by Roger Steffens) state Marley wrote it; the credit is widely explained as a way to support Ford's soup kitchen and/or to avoid a Cayman Music publishing contract. A 1987 court decision left control with the Marley estate. The 1975 Lyceum live version is the best-known recording. Year 1974 is the studio-album release year. Title in Jamaican Patois means 'Woman, don't cry'.

Nemours Jean-Baptiste (1918–1985) founded Ensemble Aux Callebasses in 1955 (renamed Ensemble Nemours Jean-Baptiste, 1957) and is credited with creating konpa dirèk. English Wikipedia biography states the 1967 composition 'Ti Carole', dedicated to a fan called Kouri, became famous. Only this source was consulted for the song itself (the genre page does not independently confirm the year), so status is Partially verified. Year 1967 is the composition year given there.

The Kitchener article says he recorded Sugar Bum Bum in 1977 and that it was a hit for the 1978 Trinidad Carnival. The Trinidad Express article reports arranger Ed Watson's claim that he supplied the beat and melody. The credited artist on the Wikipedia article is Kitchener; the melody claim is disputed and is not resolved here. Year 1977 is the recording year in the Kitchener article.

The band article lists the single New York City (1975) and says Tabou Combo was founded in Pétion-Ville, Haiti, playing compas. Swisscharts dates the Barclay single 1975 and credits music and text to Jean-Claude Jean. The band's own timeline says the song reached number one on the French hit parade in 1975. The sung language is not stated on those pages, so language is left empty. Taxonomy spelling Kompa is used for the compas/konpa the band article names.

secondary_associations: Puerto Rico | United States | Fania | Legal Alien
research_notes: The English and Spanish articles say Omar Alfanno, described as Panamanian, wrote the song in 1986 and Willie Colón recorded it with Legal Alien on the 1989 album Top Secrets. MusicBrainz dates the recording's first release 1989. Year 1986 is the composition year. Spanish Wikipedia gives the song's country of origin as Panama. Colón's New York salsa career is a secondary association, not the composition's country.

The Bandcamp album text says Weyu Larigi Weyu means Day by Day and uses a rhythm taken from dügü ritual music, with Garifuna lyrics, led by Andy Palacio. The Wikipedia album article says Wátina was released in 2007. The same text says the album is not punta-rock dance material; Punta is the taxonomy's Garifuna heading and dügü is the specific rhythm named by the source. Composer credit for this traditional-rhythm song is not separated from Palacio's leadership, so attribution is a modern setting of a ritual rhythm rather than a claim that Palacio invented the rhythm. Year 2007 is the album year.

The Bandcamp text glosses Ámuñegü as In Times to Come and quotes the song's question about who will speak Garifuna and perform the dügü and arumahani in times to come. It is a track on Wátina, which Wikipedia dates to 2007. Second Palacio title. The page does not name a separate composer, so Palacio is stored as the album's lead artist and the composition credit is not stronger than that.

The Bandcamp text says Paul Nabor, then described as 75, sings Ayó Da, a song he wrote 60 years earlier about a friend lost on a fishing trip. It does not give a calendar year, so the year field is empty. Wikipedia says Nabor appears on the 2007 album Wátina. Sixty years before an undated blurb is not converted into a year.

The English song article calls it the lead single by the Dominican artist Juan Luis Guerra and his band 4:40, language Spanish, released 1989, genre merengue. The Spanish song article names Juan Luis Guerra as autor. The English album article says the album was recorded at Estudios EMCA in Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic, and released 25 April 1989.

The English album article says Guerra composed Ángel para una Tambora in honour of the percussionist Ángel Andújar and that the album was recorded in Santo Domingo and released in 1989. The Spanish album article repeats that he composed the song. Genre Merengue is the album genre on those pages, not a separate genre label for this track. Language is not stated for this track; Spanish is the language of the title and of the companion single on the song page.
